title: Exponential Backoff + Jitter
explain: Backoff spaces retries out and jitter makes the spacing random, and you need both. Backoff alone leaves a thousand clients retrying in synchronized waves; jitter flattens those waves into a steady trickle. It is the spacing policy inside a retry budget.
model:
**Exponential backoff:** wait before retry `n` is `min(cap, base * 2^(n-1))`. With `base = 200 ms`: 200, 400, 800, 1600 ms, then the cap.

**Why backoff alone fails:** 10,000 clients fail together, all wait 200 ms, retry together, fail together, wait 400 ms... the herd stays in lockstep and the server sees spikes at 0.2 s, 0.6 s, 1.4 s. Jitter must span a **wide range**; plus or minus 10% barely spreads anything.

With `ceiling = min(cap, base * 2^(n-1))`:

| Variant | Sleep | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Full jitter** | `uniform(0, ceiling)` | best spreading, lowest server load; some retries nearly immediate |
| **Equal jitter** | `ceiling/2 + uniform(0, ceiling/2)` | guarantees a minimum wait |
| **Decorrelated** | `min(cap, uniform(base, prev*3))` | depends on the previous sleep, not the attempt number |

Rules: always a **cap** and a **max attempts or deadline**; honour `Retry-After` and still add jitter; jitter *scheduled* work (polls, cron) too. See [retry](#/sd/f/retry).

details.a: Identical clients compute identical delays, so each wave is as tall as the first; backoff only changes how far apart the waves are. Randomness is what flattens them.

details.q: Why is a plus or minus 10% jitter on a 1 s delay not a fix?
details.a: It spreads 10,000 clients over only a 0.2 s window, leaving a spike of roughly 10,000 requests per 0.2 s. The jitter range has to cover most of the delay, as full jitter does.

details.q: With base 200 ms, factor 2 and cap 5 s, what does a client sleep over its first six retries without jitter?
What is the expected sleep before retry 6 with full jitter, base 1 s, cap 30 s?
details.a: The ceiling is min(30, 32) = 30 s and uniform(0, 30) has mean 15 s.

Full jitter spreads load best and lowers total server work, but a retry can come almost immediately. Equal jitter guarantees a minimum wait at the cost of a less even spread. State which guarantee matters.

details.q: How does the deadline interact with the sleep?
details.a: Compute the sleep first, then check it against the remaining deadline, so the client never wakes up only to find there is no time left to use the retry.

details.q: Where else do you add jitter besides error retries?
details.a: Anywhere many clients act on the same schedule: periodic polls, cron-like jobs, cache expiry, token refresh. Otherwise they all hit at the top of the minute.

prompts.q: Explain exponential backoff with jitter and why you need both parts.
points: Backoff shrinks pressure as faults persist
Jitter randomizes the wait across a wide range
Cap and max attempts or deadline

prompts.q: Compare full, equal and decorrelated jitter.
10,000 clients recover from an outage at the same instant. Describe what the server sees with and without jitter.
points: Without: tall spikes at doubling intervals
Full jitter spreads over the whole interval
